title: Regret Is Weighted Forgetting
content: How much of an agent's regret comes from a bad representation, and how much from a bad policy? Here I give an exact answer. Fix a representation $M$, a function that compresses histories into states, and a finite evaluation distribution over pairs of a history and a binary diagnostic test. Sort the pairs into cells, one cell for each combination of representation state and test, so that a policy reading only the representation must answer identically across each cell. I prove that the minimum average normalised regret over all such policies equals $K_\rho(M)$, the smallest margin-weighted mass of evaluation pairs that must be deleted to leave every cell with a single optimal answer. Regret is, exactly, the cost of what the representation forces you to forget. A policy-wise decomposition then splits any actual policy's regret into this irreducible aliasing cost plus an avoidable misreporting term, in the way the bias--variance decomposition splits supervised error. The identity is stated and proved in self-contained reinforcement-learning terms, then shown to coincide, on a deliberately lifted diagnostic task, with a deficit in weighted weakness in Stack Theory, where weakness counts the unseen continuations a policy leaves open and governs how well it generalises. Off the structureless lift, weakness also sees extension structure and does not collapse into a Bayes-error quantity. The bridge yields a representation-convergence theorem, a regret-based partial order on abstractions, Lipschitz stability under margin estimation error, a multi-class generalisation, a free-energy floor, and a generalisation probability of $e^{-K_\rho(M)}$ for the optimal $M$-based policy under the canonical independent prior. Controlled POMDP experiments confirm the decomposition is numerically exact and that $K_\rho$ separates representations that accuracy and raw impurity conflate. The weakness theorems prescribe least commitment, but their formal object has no operational analogue in neural network function approximation. Future research can build on this bridge to address that gap.
